title: A rebase orphans every commit the ledger cites, and only CI notices
foundBy: rebasing the branch onto a moved main, which rewrote every commit the ledger cites
details:
`cs-ledger check` validates `evidence.commits` by asking whether the sha is a commit object in the repository. It does not ask whether any branch still contains it. A rebase rewrites every commit it replays, so the records keep pointing at the old shas, which survive as unreferenced objects on the machine that did the rebase.

So the check passes exactly where it should fail. Measured on the cs-ledger the lockfile pins, v0.0.0-20260910164917, with `ledger.html` re-rendered each time so staleness was not the thing under test:

- a sha that is no object at all fails: `evidence.commits[0] ... is not a commit in this repository`
- a sha that is an object but is contained by no branch passes: `check OK`

What decides which of those a machine sees is whether it holds the orphan. Cloning from a path copies the whole object store and carries orphans with it; cloning over the wire transfers only reachable objects and does not. CI clones over the wire. Both were run: in a wire clone the same record fails with `2fd5ceb is not a commit in this repository`.

That makes this a works-on-my-machine defect rather than a silent one. Whoever rebases sees green and CI goes red, on a repository nobody has touched since. It is visible and it is recoverable, which is the good news; it is also entirely avoidable, which is the record.

It has happened here twice, unnoticed both times. Seventeen citations across fourteen records pointed into rewritten history, the first rebase leaving CUI-080 through CUI-087 wrong while every subsequent `npm run ci` passed. They were repaired before the push, so nothing reached anyone: the `ledger check` job on a55a60e passed against a fresh clone.

notes.text:
The frequency is the point. `origin/main` moved three times during the session that filed this, so rebasing unpushed work is the normal case here rather than an event. Anything that makes a rebase cost manual repair will be paid repeatedly, and by whoever is least expecting it.

Three ways to close it, and the first is not enough on its own.

**Ask the right question.** `cs-ledger` should test that a cited commit is contained by some ref, not that it is an object: one `git merge-base --is-ancestor` per citation. That belongs in the tool, which ships as `@codesweep-ai/cs-ledger`. It does not stop citations going stale. It moves the discovery from CI to the machine that still holds the orphans, which is the only place the repair is possible.

**Make the repair mechanical.** A rebase preserves subject lines, so an orphaned citation can be matched to its replacement by subject. That is how the seventeen here were fixed, and it was deterministic: no two of the 46 commits shared a subject. A remap worth shipping refuses to guess — unique match or fail — so a commit dropped by `--skip`, or a squash that merged two subjects, stops the run rather than silently citing the wrong work.

**Or do not cite a sha until it cannot move.** The exposure exists because records are closed with the sha of a commit that is still local and therefore still rewritable. Filling `evidence.commits` only once the work is on `main` would remove the problem rather than detect it, at the cost of splitting a record's close from the work it describes, which this project has so far kept together on purpose. That trade is the decision, and it is the owner's.
